positive_controls.argument: Stable units, system boundaries and countermetrics distinguish informative feedback from a number optimized by local behavior.
Measurement boundaries and countermetrics prevent test counts or successful demonstrations from being misread as value or complete safety.
Countermetrics and comparable denominators expose priority distortions from low-risk throughput or suppressed adverse signals.
Stable boundaries, work mix and countermetrics distinguish a genuine change signal from redefinition or local metric gaming.
Outcome units, denominators, countermetrics and gaming inquiry protect the interpretation of the selected comparison.
Explicit measurement boundaries and countermetrics reveal whether a requirement’s indicator can improve while the intended outcome worsens.
Proxy and boundary inquiry identifies an assumption that must not be silently promoted to established evidence.
Comparable units, exposure denominators and countermetrics prevent a favorable demonstration count from masking unchanged system risk.
System boundaries and transferred-harm checks prevent a convenient proxy from displacing intended-use outcomes.
Stable definitions and anti-gaming checks make the comparison to agreed criteria interpretable and expose retrospective target manipulation.
Exposure denominators, reporting incentives and countermetrics challenge apparent safety gains caused by reduced reporting or shifted harm.
Boundary, denominator and gaming analysis qualifies what the numerical evidence can support and exposes selection-induced overclaims.
Countermetrics and stable problem identities distinguish actual correction from ticket splitting, severity relabeling or suppressed reports.
System countermetrics and incentive checks expose milestone gaming and apparent local success bought by hidden downstream harm.
Stable work units, boundary and incentive inquiry protect comparability of the actuals and reference class.
Reliable units, exposure boundaries and countermetrics prevent a deceptively favorable indicator from concealing accepted risk.
Boundary and denominator discipline prevents a one-dimensional score from hiding transferred harm, scarce tests or irreversible consequences.
